title: K.H. AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
summary:
In K.H. and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants were eight Slovakian women of Roma origin who brought a case against Slovakia. The women, all from the Roma community, suspected they had been sterilised without their full and informed consent during caesarean deliveries at two hospitals in eastern Slovakia. Their vulnerability lay in the serious and lasting harm of possible involuntary sterilisation, a practice that has disproportionately affected Roma women in Europe and raises profound concerns about bodily autonomy and discrimination.

Between 2002 and 2003, the applicants and their lawyers sought access to their complete medical records to investigate the cause of their infertility and to prepare potential legal claims. Despite granting powers of attorney to their legal representatives, the hospitals refused to allow photocopying of the records, citing restrictive interpretations of Slovak health law. The applicants initiated civil proceedings, but the Slovak courts upheld the hospitals’ refusal to permit photocopying, allowing only handwritten excerpts.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private life), Article 6 (right to a fair trial), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The Court found a violation of Article 8, recognising that access to personal medical information is a crucial aspect of private life, and that the refusal to allow photocopying placed an excessive burden on the applicants. This judgment is significant as it affirms the right of Roma and Traveller women to access their own medical records, a key safeguard against abuses such as forced sterilisation, and comes in the context of a troubling history of reproductive rights violations against Roma women in Central and Eastern Europe.
